# Introduction

The **rddr** package provides a robust, high-performance interface for parsing the proprietary text-based file formats used in **SAAM** and **Gasel** aviation tools.

Aviation data often comes in complex, non-standard text formats that mix hierarchical structures, geometric definitions, and pseudo-code logic. Instead of writing custom regex parsers for every analysis, **rddr** transforms `.awk`, `.flc2`, `.soa`, `.mot` and other formats into tidy `data.table`s ready for filtering and analysis.

## Supported Formats

| File Ext | Function     | Description                              |
|----------|--------------|------------------------------------------|
| `.arp`   | `read_arp`   | Airport coordinates and FIRs             |
| `.runway`| `read_runway`| Runway configurations & taxonomy         |
| `.soa`   | `read_soa`   | Area definitions (recursive groups)      |
| `.aco`   | `read_aco`   | Airspace sector colors & levels          |
| `.flc2`  | `read_flc2`  | Flight Level Constraints (FL_CONT)       |
| `.awk`   | `read_awk`   | RAD Routing Rules (REGLE)                |
| `.tax`   | `read_tax`   | Turning penalties                        |
| `.pnl`   | `read_pnl`   | Segment cost penalties                   |
| `.rlex`  | `read_rlex`  | Route length extension exceptions        |
| `.mot`   | `read_mot`   | Military/Airspace opening times          |

> **Note:** Example chunks that read external files use `eval = FALSE` so that the vignette builds even if those files are not available in your environment. Remove that option when running locally with the corresponding inputs.

# 1. Building the Network Environment

Before analyzing specific trajectories or rules, we must first load the static network definitions.

## Setup

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
```

```{r libraries}
library(rddr)
library(data.table)
```

## Airports and Coordinates

The `.arp` format stores coordinates in **minutes**. `read_arp()` automatically converts these to **decimal degrees** for immediate use in mapping.

```{r read-arp, eval=FALSE}
# Load Airport Definitions
airports <- read_arp("data/network.arp")

# Preview
head(airports)
#    icao     lat      lon     fir_id
# 1: EBBR 50.9014   4.4844   EBBU_FIR
# 2: LFPG 49.0097   2.5479   LFFF_FIR
```

## Area Definitions (Groups)

The `.soa` format defines groups of airports (e.g., `LONDON_GROUP`). These definitions are often **recursive** (a group containing other groups). Use `resolve_recursion = TRUE` to **flatten** these hierarchies instantly.

```{r read-soa, eval=FALSE}
# Read Area Groups
areas <- read_soa("data/groups.soa", resolve_recursion = TRUE)

# Find all airports in the "SCANDINAVIA" group
scandi_airports <- areas[area_id == "SCANDINAVIA", member_id]
```

## Sectors and Runways

Visualizing sectors and understanding runway constraints are key for capacity analysis.

```{r read-aco-runway, eval=FALSE}
# Read Sector Colors (returns RGBA and Hex codes)
sectors <- read_aco("data/airspace.aco")

# Read Runway configurations
runways <- read_runway("data/airport.runway")
```

# 2. Analyzing Logic: RAD Rules & Constraints

A powerful feature of **rddr** is parsing the pseudo-code logic found in `.flc2` (Level Constraints) and `.awk` (Routing) files. These files can contain complex `if`/`then` logic, nested blocks, and regex matching.

## Parsing Flight Level Constraints (`.flc2`)

Instead of treating rule code as simple text strings, set `parse_rules = TRUE` to extract actionable columns like `DEP`, `ARR`, and `FL_CONT`.

```{r read-flc2, eval=FALSE}
# Parse Flight Level Constraints
# This handles nested 'if' blocks and extracts regex patterns
flc <- read_flc2("data/constraints.flc2", parse_rules = TRUE)

# Inspect the structured output
head(flc[, .(rule_id, condition_dep, condition_arr, constraint_type, constraint_value)])
```

### Practical Example: Filtering Rules for a Flight

Imagine you are analyzing a flight from Brussels (**EBBR**) to Paris (**LFPG**). You want to know which flight level constraints apply.

```{r flc-filter, eval=FALSE}
# Define flight parameters
my_dep <- "EBBR"
my_arr <- "LFPG"

# Filter active rules that match our flight
applicable_rules <- flc[
  is_active == TRUE &
  (is.na(condition_dep) | grepl(condition_dep, my_dep)) &
  (is.na(condition_arr) | grepl(condition_arr, my_arr))
]

applicable_rules[, .(rule_id, constraint_type, constraint_value)]
# Example output: 
#       rule_id constraint_type constraint_value
# 1: SAAM_R001             MAX              245
# 2: SAAM_R055             MIN              195
```

## Parsing Routing Rules (`.awk`)

Routing rules are similar but often involve `REGLE` (routing strings) and `RFL` (Requested Flight Level) conditions.

```{r read-awk, eval=FALSE}
rad_rules <- read_awk("data/routing.awk", parse_rules = TRUE)

# Find rules that force a specific routing for heavy jets (RFL >= 300)
# flying out of the London area
forced_routes <- rad_rules[
  constraint_type == "ROUTING" &
  condition_rfl_min >= 300 &
  grepl("EG[A-Z]{2}", condition_dep)
]

# View the enforced routing string
head(forced_routes[, .(rule_id, routing_constraint)])
```

# 3. Handling Penalties and Exceptions

For optimization or simulation workflows, you often need to load costs and exceptions.

## Turn Penalties (`.tax`)

The `.tax` file defines geometric penalties for specific turns (Point1 -> Point2 -> Point3).

```{r read-tax, eval=FALSE}
turns <- read_tax("data/penalties.tax")

# Check if turning at 'ADUTO' coming from 'KOK' carries a penalty
turns[point_1 == "KOK" & point_2 == "ADUTO"]
```

## Military Opening Times (`.mot`)

The `read_mot()` reader handles versions 1, 2, and 3 of the format automatically, standardizing opening times and level restrictions.

```{r read-mot, eval=FALSE}
mil_areas <- read_mot("data/military.mot")

# Filter for areas active during the morning peak
morning_active <- mil_areas[start_time <= "0800" & end_time >= "0900"]
```

# 4. Summary

The **rddr** package abstracts away the complexity of parsing legacy text formats. By converting everything into `data.table` structures, it allows analysts to focus on traffic flow, rule compliance, and network optimization rather than regular expressions and low-level file parsing.
